title: Sitting and forgetting
hook: Zhuangzi's Yan Hui "sits and forgets" everything, even himself (Zhuangzi 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sangat: the Sikh company of the holy, where nobody has a better seat. Your line was good company. Did you make that plan with the person you pictured? Day one thousand four hundred three.

A student walks up to his teacher with news. I'm making progress, he says. The teacher asks what he means. I've forgotten goodness and duty, the student says. The teacher nods. Good. But not yet. Some days later the student is back. I'm making progress. I've forgotten ritual and music. Good, says the teacher. But not yet. Then the student comes a third time, and this time the teacher is the one who is startled. The student is Yan Hui. The teacher is Confucius. And the book telling the story belongs to neither of them. It's the Zhuangzi, a Daoist classic, and today's word is what Yan Hui says on that third visit.
screen: `I'M MAKING PROGRESS.` → `GOOD. BUT NOT YET.` → `THE THIRD VISIT.`

segments.voice: On the third visit Yan Hui says: I sit and forget. In Chinese, zuowang. Confucius, the story says, looks startled and asks what that means. Yan Hui answers, in plain paraphrase: I let my limbs and body drop away. I dismiss my hearing and my sight. I leave behind my form, I put away what I know, and I become one with the great road that runs through everything. That, he says, is sitting and forgetting. And then comes the turn. Confucius, the famous teacher, says: if you are one with it, you have no likes; if you are changed by it, you hold nothing fixed. You really are worthy. Please let me follow behind you. The teacher asks to become the student. Look at the order of what gets forgotten. First goodness and duty. Then ritual and music. These are not bad things; they are the very things Confucius taught. Yan Hui puts down even the good lists, and then he puts down the one keeping the lists. Readers take this in more than one way. Some hear a method: a real sitting practice, emptying the mind until only stillness is left, and some later Daoists took it up that way. Others hear a joke with a point: here Zhuangzi puts words in Confucius's mouth, and lets the great teacher of rules bow to a student who has let the rules go. Either way, the story is gentle about it. Yan Hui doesn't fight his thoughts. He forgets them, the way you forget a coat on a warm day. You just stop carrying it.
screen: `I SIT AND FORGET.` · `BODY, SENSES, KNOWING: LET GO.` · `THE TEACHER ASKS TO FOLLOW.` · `EVEN THE GOOD LISTS GO DOWN.` · then, large: `PLEASE LET ME FOLLOW BEHIND YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit and let go of lists. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Your mind will offer a list: things to do, things you forgot, things you should have said. Don't fight it, and don't finish it. Just notice: a list. Then let it go, the way you'd set a bag down. Let the body be heavy. Let sounds come and go without naming them. If another list arrives, set that one down too. Nothing to achieve here. Only less to carry. The bell holds the time.
Zuowang. Sitting and forgetting, from the Zhuangzi: letting go of body, senses and knowing, until only the great road is left. Today's word.

Your line: sit and forget. Today, when a list starts running in your head, pause before you add to it. Set it down for three breaths, and see what is still there without it. Day one thousand four hundred three.

howItsDone: Readers of the Zhuangzi meet zuowang in the story of Yan Hui and Confucius, and some Daoist practitioners treat sitting and forgetting as a meditation: sitting still and letting thoughts, senses and self-concern fall away.

fork.setup: you're Confucius. your student Yan Hui says, I sit and forget, and explains he has let go of body, senses and knowing. what do you say?
options: scold him for forgetting your teaching.
tell him, good, but not yet.
call him worthy and ask to follow behind him.
fork.reveal: in the Zhuangzi, Confucius says Yan Hui is truly worthy and asks to follow behind him. the teacher becomes the student.

what a scholar hears: a Daoist book making Confucius bow to his student, and a phrase some later Daoists turned into a sitting method.

notes: Zhuangzi 6 is paraphrased throughout (Legge 1891 renders it, but his exact wording was not checked). Confirm the order of what Yan Hui forgets (ren and yi first, then rites and music, in the received text) and the paraphrase of Confucius's reply ('one, no likes; transformed, no constancy; please let me follow behind you').
'The great road that runs through everything' paraphrases 同於大通; Legge has 'the Great Pervader'. Confirm the plain rendering.
'Later Daoists wrote whole guides on it' refers to later Daoist texts on zuowang (e.g. the Zuowang lun); no author or date given under the claims rule. Confirm or cut.
'Zhuangzi loved to put words in Confucius's mouth' is a general reading of the book's style; confirm the framing is fair to both traditions.

Editor pass: 'later Daoists wrote whole guides on it' softened to 'some later Daoists took it up that way'; 'Zhuangzi loved to put words in Confucius's mouth' (a claim about the whole book) narrowed to this story, in the teach and the myth reveal.
